chapters.name: Sign Shapes, Colors, and Regulatory Signs
chapters.summary: How shape and color tell you what a sign means, and the red, white, and black signs that state rules you must obey.
keyPoints: The eight-sided sign is used only for STOP. The triangle with its point at the bottom is used only for YIELD.
Rectangular and square signs in black and white or red and white show speed limits and other rules, such as NO U-TURN or KEEP RIGHT EXCEPT TO PASS.
A red circle with a slash means the action shown inside it is not allowed.

chapters.name: Warning, School, Railroad, and Work Zone Signs
chapters.summary: Yellow diamond warning signs, the no-passing pennant, the school pentagon, railroad crossing signs, and orange work zone signs.
keyPoints: Diamond-shaped signs warn of a hazard or a change in the road ahead. They are black on yellow, or black on orange in work zones.
The yellow pennant on the left side of the road marks the start of a no-passing zone.
The five-sided sign means a school zone or school crossing. The round yellow RR sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead.

chapters.name: Guide Signs and Route Markers
chapters.summary: Green, blue, and brown guide signs, and the shapes used to mark Interstate, U.S., and North Carolina routes.
keyPoints: Interstate routes use a red, white, and blue shield. U.S. routes use a shield, and North Carolina routes use a diamond.
Odd-numbered highways generally run north and south. Even-numbered highways generally run east and west.
Blue and white signs point to services such as a hospital or a Highway Patrol station.

chapters.name: Traffic Signals and Pavement Markings
chapters.summary: Steady and flashing lights, turn arrows, hybrid beacons and ramp meters, and what yellow and white lines and colored pavement markers mean.
keyPoints: A flashing red light means the same as a STOP sign. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after you yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
If a signal is not working, treat the intersection as if there were a stop sign on every approach.
Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going the same way. If the yellow edge line is on your right, you are going the wrong way.

chapters.name: Right of Way, School Buses, and Emergency Vehicles
chapters.summary: Who goes first at intersections, roundabouts, and driveways, how to treat pedestrians, and what to do for school buses, emergency vehicles, and trains.
keyPoints: When two vehicles reach an intersection without signs or signals at the same time, the vehicle on the right has the right of way.
On a two-lane road or a four-lane road with no median, traffic from both directions must stop for a stopped school bus.
For an emergency vehicle stopped within 12 feet of the road with its lights on, move out of the lane next to it, or slow down if you cannot change lanes.

chapters.name: Speed, Passing, and Parking
chapters.summary: North Carolina's speed limits, following distance, safe and legal passing, backing, turn signals, and the places where you may not park.
keyPoints: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit is 35 mph in cities and towns and 55 mph outside them. The highest limit on interstates is 70 mph.
Do not pass on a hill or curve where you cannot see at least 500 feet ahead. Pass at least 2 feet to the left of the vehicle you pass.
Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or within 25 feet of the curb line of an intersecting street.

chapters.name: Safe Driving, Emergencies, and Sharing the Road
chapters.summary: Headlights, rain, fog, snow, skids and other emergencies, crashes, seat belts and child seats, and sharing the road with trucks, bicycles, and motorcycles.
keyPoints: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise, when you cannot see 400 feet ahead, and whenever you use your wipers because of bad weather.
If your car starts to hydroplane, ease off the gas, do not brake hard, and keep the wheel straight.
A crash must be reported to law enforcement if anyone is hurt or killed or damage appears to be $1,000 or more.

chapters.name: Learner Permit and Graduated Licensing
chapters.summary: The three levels of North Carolina's graduated license for drivers under 18, the supervising driver, and the rules for cell phones and passengers.
keyPoints: A Level 1 limited learner permit is for ages 15 to 17 after driver education. For the first six months you may drive only from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. with your supervising driver.
You must hold the Level 1 permit for nine months and log at least 60 hours of driving, with 10 at night, before the Level 2 license.
A driver under 18 may not use a cell phone while driving except to call for help in an emergency.

chapters.name: Alcohol, DWI, and the Point System
chapters.summary: North Carolina's alcohol limits, implied consent, the penalties for DWI, and how driver license points can lead to a suspension.
keyPoints: A driver 21 or older is impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more. A driver under 21 may not drive with any alcohol in the body.
Refusing a chemical test brings an immediate revocation of at least 30 days and a further revocation of at least 12 months.
Twelve points within three years can suspend your license. Passing a stopped school bus costs 5 points.
